TOPICS.title: Partial derivatives and directional slopes
TOPICS.overview: Holding one input fixed gives a slope through a surface. This section distinguishes that coordinate slope from the change in an arbitrary unit direction, and explains when mixed derivatives agree.

DERIVATIONS.not_applicable: The formulas are demonstrated through worked differentiation rather than a separate proof.

TOPICS.title: Total change and the chain rule
TOPICS.overview: When both inputs change, their contributions combine. The total differential estimates a small finite change, while the chain rule gives the exact derivative of the composed function along a differentiable path.

DERIVATIONS.not_applicable: The formulas are demonstrated through worked differentiation rather than a separate proof.

TOPICS.title: Implicit curves and valid tangent formulas
TOPICS.overview: An equation can define a curve without giving y explicitly. Differentiate the relation, check that the point lies on the curve, and confirm the denominator is nonzero before evaluating a slope.

DEFS.text: The derivative with respect to one coordinate while all other independent coordinates remain fixed.
A vector of length one. Normalise a supplied direction before using $D_{\mathbf u}f=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u$.
The linear part of the change in a differentiable function, $df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy$.
The one-variable function obtained after replacing every changing input by its path expression.
An equation $F(x,y)=0$ that describes admissible pairs $(x,y)$.
A local representation of the curve as a differentiable function $y(x)$, justified here by $F_y\ne0$.

POINTS.text: Differentiate before substituting the evaluation point. Substitution too early can erase the variable that must change.
A path can change several inputs at once; include one chain-rule term for each changing input.
Verify the point belongs to the relation and the chosen denominator is nonzero before evaluating an implicit derivative.

WHY.q: Why can the same surface have two coordinate slopes?
WHY.a: An x-section and a y-section follow different curves through the same point, so their slopes need not agree.

WHY.q: Why does a differential differ from a finite change?
WHY.a: The differential keeps the linear part. Nonlinear terms remain in the exact finite increment.

WHY.q: Why does a zero denominator require a new analysis?
WHY.a: It prevents division in the chosen formula. The curve may instead have a vertical tangent or fail to be regular; examine the defining equation.

TRAPS.text: The gradient is a vector. A directional slope is the dot product of that vector with a unit direction.
Do not write a finite-change approximation as an exact equality. State the base point and the increments.
Do not evaluate a tangent at a point that is not on the curve. Do not turn division by zero into a slope of zero.

WORKED.title: Read two coordinate slopes
steps: Hold $y$ fixed to get $f_x=2xy$. Hold $x$ fixed to get $f_y=x^2+\cos y$.
Substitute the point only after differentiating: $f_x(1,0)=0$ and $f_y(1,0)=1+1$.
WORKED.check: The x-section at y=0 is identically zero. The y-section has slope 2 at the point.

WORKED.title: Choose an oblique direction
WORKED.check: The direction is a unit vector; no further scaling is needed.

WORKED.title: Estimate a finite change
steps: The gradient at the base point is $(0,2)$.
Direct evaluation gives $\Delta f\approx-0.0204038333$; compare it with the linear estimate.
WORKED.check: The absolute discrepancy is about 0.0004038333, which is a higher-order remainder.

WORKED.title: Find the tangent to a circle
steps: Evaluate $y^{\prime}=-x/y=-3/4$ and use the point-slope equation.
WORKED.check: The radius vector $(3,4)$ is perpendicular to tangent direction $(4,-3)$ because their dot product is zero.

WORKED.title: Recognise a vertical tangent
steps: Check $5^2+0^2=25$, so the point lies on the curve.
The denominator $F_y=2y$ is zero; the formula for $dy/dx$ cannot be evaluated.
WORKED.answer: The tangent is the vertical line $x=5$.
WORKED.check: Changing the dependent variable gives a regular local description; a zero denominator is not a zero slope.

NOTES.text: A partial derivative changes one coordinate while holding the others fixed. It is the slope of the corresponding surface section. The gradient collects these coordinate slopes, and its dot product with a unit vector gives the directional derivative. Mixed partials agree under suitable continuity assumptions.

For a differentiable function, the total differential combines the coordinate contributions to first-order change. Along a differentiable path, the chain rule gives the exact derivative of the composition. Check the result by direct substitution when that route is practical.

Implicit differentiation applies the chain rule to a relation. For a regular branch with nonzero F_y, the slope is minus F_x divided by F_y. The equation itself validates the evaluation point. A zero denominator may indicate that x should be treated as a function of y instead.

DERIVATIONS.title: Derive the second derivative on the circle
steps: Differentiate again using the product rule: $2+2(y^{\prime})^2+2yy^{\prime\prime}=0$.
DERIVATIONS.check: On the upper semicircle y is positive, so the second derivative is negative, as its concave-down shape requires.

PRACTICE.title: A claim about gradients
PRACTICE.prompt: True or false: the gradient itself is the scalar slope in every direction.
steps: A gradient contains one component per independent coordinate.
Choose a unit direction and take a dot product to obtain its scalar slope.
PRACTICE.check: Compare the x and y slopes in W1.1.

PRACTICE.title: A missing chain-rule path
PRACTICE.prompt: A student differentiates $z=x^2y$ along $x=t^2$, $y=1+t$ and writes $z^{\prime}=2xy(2t)$. Find and repair the omission.
steps: The student included the x path but omitted the y path.

PRACTICE.title: Circle second derivative
steps: Substitute $y=4$ after checking the point and denominator.
PRACTICE.check: The negative second derivative agrees with the concave-down upper semicircle.
